source_text: Nunc argumenta eorum qui contra disserunt refellamus: quae Lucretius tertio libro executus est. quoniam cum corpore inquit anima nascitur, cum corpore intereat necesse est. at non est par utriusque ratio. solidum enim et conprehensibile corpus est et oculis et manu, anima uero tenuis et tactum uisumque fugiens. corpus e terra fictum atque solidatum est, anima nihil in se concreti, nihil ponderis terreni habet, ut Plato disserebat. nec enim tantam posset habere sollertiam, tantam uim, tantam celeritatem, nisi originem traheret e caelo. corpus igitur quoniam fictum ex ponderoso et corruptibili elemento et tangibile est et uisibile, corrumpitur atque occidit nec uim repellere potest, quia sub aspectum et sub tactum uenit, anima autem quia tenuitate sua omnem tactum fugit, nullo ictu dissolui potest. ergo quamuis inter se coniuncta et sociata nascantur et alterum, quod est de terrena concretione formatum, quasi uasculum sit alterius, quod est a caelesti suptilitate deductum, cum uis aliqua utrumque discreuerit, quae discretio mors uocatur, utrumque in naturam suam recedit: quod ex terra fuit, id in terram resoluitur, quod ex caelesti spiritu, id constat ac uiget semper, quoniam diuinus spiritus sempiternus est. denique idem Lucretius oblitus quid adsereret et quod dogma defenderet, hos uersus posuit: cedit item retro, de terra quod fuit ante, in terram, sed quod missum est ex aetheris oris, id rursum caeli fulgentia templa receptant. quod eius non erat dicere qui perire animas cum corporibus disserebat: sed uictus est ueritate et inprudenti ratio uera subrepsit. praeterea id ipsum quod colligit, dissolui animam, hoc est simul cum corpore interire, quoniam simul nascantur, et falsum est et in contrarium conuerti potest. non enim simul interit, sed anima discedente integrum per multos dies manet et plerumque medicatum diutissime durat. nam si ut simul nascuntur, simul interirent, non discederet repente anima corpusque desereret, sed uno temporis puncto utrumque pariter dissiparetur et tam celeriter etiam corpus adhuc spiritu in eo manente deliquesceret ac periret, quam celeriter anima secedit, immo uero dissoluto corpore anima uanesceret uelut umor fracto uase diffusus. nam si terrenum et tragile corpus post secessum animae non statim diffluit in terramque tabescit, ei qua illi origo est, ergo anima, quae fragilis non est, in aeternum manet, quoniam origo eius aeterna est.
pass_a_gloss: Now let us refute the arguments of those who discourse against us, which Lucretius executed in his third book. Since, he says, the soul is born with the body, it is necessary that it also perish with the body. But the reasoning of both is not equal. For the body is solid and tangible, and is perceived by the eyes and the hand, but the soul is subtle and flees from touch and sight. The body is fashioned and solidified from the earth, but the soul has nothing concrete in itself, no earthly weight, as Plato used to say. For it could not have such great skill, such great power, such great swiftness, unless it drew its origin from heaven. Therefore, since the body, fashioned from a heavy and corruptible element, is tangible and visible, it is corrupted and dies and cannot repel force, because it comes under sight and touch, but the soul, because it flees all touch by its subtlety, cannot be dissolved by any blow. Therefore, although they are born connected and associated with each other, and one, which is formed from earthly concretion, is like a vessel for the other, which is derived from heavenly subtlety, when some force separates both, which separation is called death, both return to their own nature: what was from the earth is resolved into the earth, what was from the heavenly spirit remains and thrives always, because the divine spirit is eternal. Finally, the same Lucretius, forgetful of what he was asserting and what dogma he was defending, placed these verses: It also yields, what was from the earth before, to the earth, but what was sent from the shores of the ether, this the shining temples of heaven receive again. Which was not for him to say who was discoursing that souls perish with bodies: but he was conquered by the truth and the true reason slipped in unaware. Moreover, that very thing which he gathers, that the soul is dissolved, that is, it perishes at the same time as the body, because they are born at the same time, is false and can be turned to the contrary. For the body does not perish at the same time, but remains intact for many days after the soul has departed, and often, having been treated with medicine, it endures for a very long time. For if, just as they are born at the same time, they were to perish at the same time, the soul would not suddenly depart and the body would not be deserted, but both would be dissipated at the same moment of time and the body would also melt away and perish as quickly as the soul departs, but in truth, with the body dissolved, the soul vanishes like a liquid diffused from a broken vessel. For if the earthly and fragile body does not immediately dissolve into the earth and decay after the departure of the soul, because it has that origin, therefore the soul, which is not fragile, remains forever, because its origin is eternal.

pass_b_english: Let us now refute the arguments of those who argue against us, arguments that Lucretius set out in his third book. He says that since the soul is born with the body, it must necessarily perish with the body. But the reasoning for the two is not equal. The body is solid and tangible, perceived by both eyes and hand, while the soul is subtle and eludes both touch and sight. The body is fashioned and solidified from the earth; the soul has nothing concrete in itself, no earthly weight, as Plato used to say. For it could not possess such great skill, such great power, such great swiftness unless it drew its origin from heaven. Therefore, because the body is formed from a heavy and corruptible element, it is tangible and visible; it decays and dies and cannot repel force, since it falls under both sight and touch. But the soul, because by its subtlety it flees all touch, cannot be dissolved by any blow. Thus, although they are born connected and united, and the one formed from earthly concretion serves as a kind of vessel for the other derived from heavenly subtlety, when some force separates them—a separation called death—each returns to its own nature: what came from earth dissolves back into earth, and what came from the heavenly spirit endures and thrives forever, because the divine spirit is eternal.

Finally, Lucretius himself, forgetting what he was asserting and what dogma he was defending, wrote these lines: "It yields back to the earth what was from the earth before, but what was sent from the shores of the ether, the shining temples of heaven receive again." That was not something he ought to have said, he who argued that souls perish with bodies; but he was conquered by the truth, and true reason slipped in unawares. Moreover, the very conclusion he draws—that the soul is dissolved, that is, perishes at the same time as the body because they are born at the same time—is false and can be turned to the contrary. For the body does not perish at the same time; it remains intact for many days after the soul has departed, and often, when treated with medicine, it endures for a very long time. If, just as they are born together, they were to perish together, the soul would not suddenly depart and leave the body deserted; instead both would dissipate at the same moment, and the body would melt away and perish as quickly as the soul departs—indeed, with the body dissolved, the soul would vanish like liquid spilled from a broken vessel. But if the earthly and fragile body does not immediately dissolve into the earth and decay after the soul's departure, because it has that origin, then the soul, which is not fragile, remains forever, because its origin is eternal.
